chapter_title: Wisdom Paves the Way (Wit and Wisdom)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 5 periods = 225 minutes
Total: 5 periods · 3h 45min

periods.activity_title: Reading the Play Aloud and Scene I Comprehension

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.32): complete sentences giving reasons for characters' speeches.
Let us think and reflect (p.37–38): extract questions on Extract 1 — character and word meaning.

time_bands.activity: Read the play 'Wisdom Paves the Way' aloud — teacher and students share roles, following the script. Pause briefly after each character's deduction to let students absorb the observation being made.

Using 'Let us discuss' (p.32), pairs complete the sentence-completion task giving reasons for Dev Datt's, Har Datt's, Shiv Datt's, the merchant's, and Dev Datt's second speech. Pairs share answers aloud and the class settles on the best wording.

Work through Extract 1 questions from 'Let us think and reflect' (p.37–38): identify the false statement and correct it, discuss what Ram Datt's confidence reveals, and tackle the two multiple-choice questions on 'press on' and Har Datt's character.

periods.teacher_notes: The play hinges on four distinct reasoning chains — lame leg, blind eye, short tail, stomach ailment — so during shared reading, ask each student reader to slow down at the deduction line and let the class see the logical step. A common difficulty is conflating the merchant's suspicion (emotional response) with the young men's deductions (evidence-based reasoning); the sentence-completion task is a good moment to draw that contrast explicitly.
materials: Textbook pp.27–39 (play text and Let us discuss, Let us think and reflect exercises)

periods.activity_title: Scene II Court Questions and Reflective Discussion

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.36–37): sequence Scene II events in correct order.
Let us think and reflect (p.38): Extract 2 questions — assertion-reason, phrase meaning, fill-in.
Let us think and reflect (p.39): short-answer questions on journey, merchant's suspicion, and the King's judgement.

time_bands.activity: Students arrange the eight Scene II events ('Let us discuss', p.36–37) in order of occurrence, working individually then comparing with a partner. Class consensus is reached by calling on pairs to justify each placement.

Work through Extract 2 from 'Let us think and reflect' (p.38): the assertion-reason MCQ, the 'see beyond the obvious' MCQ, the fill-in on Ram Datt's reaction, and a brief class discussion on how the King's offer reflects his values as a ruler.

Open discussion using selected questions from 'Let us think and reflect' (p.39): the dusty road as symbol of challenge, why the merchant grew suspicious, and why the King trusted the four men. Students respond in two or three sentences and the class builds a shared interpretation.

periods.teacher_notes: The sequence task for Scene II is a useful check on whether students have tracked the court proceedings; if several students place the merchant's accusation after the King's questions, revisit the play's stage directions together. The assertion-reason item is often the first such format students encounter — worth spending a moment explaining that (R) must explain (A), not merely co-exist with it.
materials: Textbook pp.36–39 (Let us discuss, Let us think and reflect)

periods.activity_title: Listening to Witty Characters; Sentence Stress and Intonation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.42): match six statements to four speakers; two statements unused.
Let us speak (p.43): stress-shift exercise — say each 'I take my dog' sentence, explain meaning change.
Let us speak (p.43): practise four play sentences with correct falling intonation.

time_bands.activity: Read the transcript for 'Let us listen' (p.48) aloud twice as students listen — once for gist, once while they note key words. Students then match the six statements (p.42) to speakers (i)–(iv), identifying the two unused statements, and pairs compare answers before class confirmation.

Introduce word stress using 'Let us speak' (p.43): teacher models each version of 'I take my dog for a walk in the evening' with a different stressed word. Pairs take turns producing each version and explain to each other how the emphasis shifts the meaning.

Practise falling intonation on the four sentences from the play (p.43). Teacher models once; students repeat chorally, then individually. The class discusses why statements and exclamations carry falling rather than rising tone.

periods.teacher_notes: For the listening task, read each speaker's passage at a measured pace — the statements to be matched paraphrase the speakers rather than quoting them exactly, so students need to listen for meaning, not word-for-word recall. In the stress exercise, students often assume stress is purely about volume; guide them to see that pitch and length also mark the stressed syllable.
materials: Textbook pp.42–43 (Let us listen, Let us speak)

periods.activity_title: Formal Letter of Complaint and Vocabulary from the Play

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.44): draft formal complaint letter — road damage, consequences, suggestions.
Let us learn (p.39): fill in noun forms of textual words (deduce, observe, scrutinise, accuse, recognise).
Let us learn (p.39–40): match eight play expressions to their meanings.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.40): write sentences using any five expressions from the matched list.

time_bands.activity: Introduce noun derivation using 'Let us learn' (p.39): students fill in the noun forms of the five bracketed words from the play. Teacher elicits answers and discusses how these nouns appear in the play's dialogue.

Students match the eight idiomatic expressions from the play ('Let us learn', p.39–40) to their meanings in Column 2. Pairs compare, then the teacher confirms answers, pausing on expressions like 'grand scheme of things' and 'more than meets the eye' to show how they enrich the play's dialogue.

Guided writing: teacher displays the three-paragraph format for a formal complaint letter ('Let us write', p.44). Students plan briefly — issue, details and consequences, suggestions — then draft the full letter to the Commissioner or Sarpanch. Teacher circulates, prompting correct salutation, subject line, and formal register.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse the noun forms of 'scrutinise' (scrutiny) and 'recognise' (recognition); draw attention to the irregular suffixes before the fill-in. For the letter, the context in the play — the young men's calm, evidence-based approach to the King — is a useful model for the measured, factual tone a formal complaint requires; make that link explicit.
materials: Textbook pp.39–44 (Let us learn, Let us write)

periods.activity_title: Modal Verbs in Context and Play Enactment Planning

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.41): match eleven modal verb sentences to their grammatical functions.
Let us learn (p.42): fill in modal verbs in the wisdom story using function clues.
Let us explore (p.44–45): plan and begin enacting 'Wisdom Paves the Way' with correct stress and intonation.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.42): rewrite sentences 2–5 replacing highlighted phrases with appropriate modal verbs.

time_bands.activity: Students match the eleven modal verb sentences from 'Let us learn' (p.41) to their functions. Teacher works through two or three contrasting pairs (e.g., 'must' for logical conclusion vs. 'must' for obligation) to establish that context determines function.

Students complete the modal verb fill-in story ('Let us learn', p.42) using the function clues in brackets. Answers are shared aloud; the class discusses why 'might' rather than 'must' fits 'weak possibility' and similar distinctions.

Introduce the play enactment project ('Let us explore', p.44–45): the class assigns roles for 'Wisdom Paves the Way' and rehearses key scenes in groups, applying the sentence stress and falling intonation practised earlier. Groups perform their assigned scene for the class and receive brief feedback on delivery.

periods.teacher_notes: The modal verb matching task draws on sentences taken directly from the play, so students can return to those lines in their scripts for context — this is especially useful for distinguishing 'would' as imagined possibility from 'would' as prediction. For the enactment, groups do not need elaborate props; the focus is on vocal delivery, so any space in the classroom where students can face their audience is sufficient.
materials: Textbook pp.41–45 (Let us learn modal verbs, Let us explore)

items.source_lo: Student analyses a dramatic dialogue by identifying characters' reasoning processes and evaluating evidence-based conclusions using the dialogue as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Four young men deduce camel's traits from tracks; King vindicates them in court.
items.item_stem: Which of the following correctly identifies the physical evidence Ram Datt used to deduce that the camel was lame in one leg?

options.label: A
options.text: One of the camel's footprints was fainter than the other three.

options.label: B
options.text: Small droplets of blood appeared at intervals along the track.

options.label: C
options.text: The camel had eaten foliage only from one side of the road.

options.label: D
options.text: The camel's forefeet prints were deeper than the hind feet prints.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses Ram Datt's observation with Shiv Datt's, who noted the one-sided grazing pattern.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses Ram Datt's observation with Har Datt's, who noted the blood droplets indicating a short tail.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses Ram Datt's observation with Dev Datt's, who noted the deeper forefoot prints indicating a stomach ailment.

items.source_lo: Student analyses a dramatic dialogue by identifying characters' reasoning processes and evaluating evidence-based conclusions using the dialogue as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Four young men deduce camel's traits from tracks; King vindicates them in court.
items.item_stem: In Scene II, the King listens carefully to each young man's explanation before dismissing the merchant's accusation and offering all four men positions as royal advisers. What does the King's conduct in court reveal about the kind of ruler he is, and how does the play use this moment to comment on the value of evidence-based reasoning over hasty judgement?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The King's methodical questioning and willingness to hear each man's reasoning before ruling shows him to be just, patient, and intellectually discerning. The play uses this moment to argue that a wise ruler values logic and careful observation over emotional accusation, rewarding the men's evidence-based thinking with the highest honour his court can offer.

items.source_context: Four speakers share views on witty characters in stories; two statements unused.
items.item_stem: Speaker (i) and Speaker (iii) both admire witty characters, yet their reasons are different. After listening to both speakers, write two or three sentences explaining what distinguishes Speaker (i)'s admiration from Speaker (iii)'s, using specific details from what each speaker says.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Speaker (i) admires witty characters primarily because they make tense situations funny and think fast to solve problems without panicking. Speaker (iii) admires them because they use humour instead of fighting and, specifically in folktales, show that smart thinking can defeat force — an additional lesson that also keeps the listener calm in difficult real-life situations.

items.source_context: Stress-shift sentences and falling intonation on play lines from Scene I and II.
items.item_stem: Say the following sentence aloud three times, each time stressing the underlined word. After each reading, describe in one sentence how the meaning changes: (a) I spotted the camel's tracks on the road. (b) I spotted the camel's tracks on the road. (c) I spotted the camel's tracks on the road.

expected_elements: Clearly shifts stress to the underlined word in each reading.
Explains that stressing 'I' means the speaker (not someone else) spotted them.
Explains that stressing 'camel's' specifies whose tracks, not another animal's.
Explains that stressing 'road' distinguishes the location from elsewhere.

items.source_lo: Student applies knowledge of word stress and sentence intonation to convey precise meaning in spoken English using guided oral practice as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Stress-shift sentences and falling intonation on play lines from Scene I and II.
items.item_stem: You are playing the merchant in Scene I of 'Wisdom Paves the Way'. Your camel is missing and you have just met the four young men who describe it accurately. Deliver four lines of dialogue in role — accusing them and demanding they come before the King — using falling intonation on your exclamatory and declarative lines. Your partner plays one of the four young men responding calmly. After the role-play, explain to the class why falling intonation sounds more authoritative than a rising tone in this context.

expected_elements: Uses falling intonation on declarative and exclamatory lines consistently.
Dialogue is in role and reflects the merchant's suspicion and urgency.
Partner's response reflects the young men's calm dignity under accusation.
Explanation connects falling tone to authority and finality in speech.

items.source_lo: Student composes a structured formal complaint letter using a civic context drawn from the dialogue's theme as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Formal letter to Commissioner or Sarpanch about damaged kutcha road; three-paragraph format.
items.item_stem: Write a formal letter to the Sarpanch of your Gram Panchayat complaining about a damaged kutcha road in your colony. Your letter must follow the standard formal letter format (sender's address, date, designation and address of recipient, subject line, salutation, body paragraphs, complimentary close and signature). In paragraph one, state your purpose and describe the problem. In paragraph two, explain the consequences — including the risk of accidents and mosquito breeding. In paragraph three, suggest remedies and request swift action.

expected_elements: Correct formal letter format: address, date, subject line, salutation.
Paragraph 1 clearly states purpose and names the specific problem.
Paragraph 2 gives concrete consequences — accidents and mosquito breeding.
Paragraph 3 suggests at least one remedy and uses appropriately formal register.

items.source_lo: Student composes a structured formal complaint letter using a civic context drawn from the dialogue's theme as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Formal letter to Commissioner or Sarpanch about damaged kutcha road; three-paragraph format.
items.item_stem: Imagine you are Dev Datt, now serving as one of the King's royal advisers. The King has asked you to write a short report — in the form of a formal advisory note — recommending that the road leading into Ujjain be repaired before the next trading season. Write your advisory note (approximately 120 words) stating the problem clearly, giving two specific reasons why the road's condition harms the kingdom's interests, and proposing one practical course of action. Use appropriately formal language throughout.

expected_elements: Adopts a formal advisory register suited to a royal court context.
States the road problem clearly with at least two specific consequences for the kingdom.
Proposes a practical, specific course of action for repair.
Connects the task to the play's theme of evidence-based reasoning and wise counsel.

items.source_context: Noun derivation (deduce/observe/accuse), idiomatic expressions, modal verb functions from play sentences.
items.item_stem:
The play 'Wisdom Paves the Way' is full of moments where characters make careful observations and logical deductions. Complete each sentence below by writing the correct noun form of the verb given in parentheses, and then write one original sentence of your own using any two of those noun forms together.
1. The four men's _________________ (observe) of the camel tracks was detailed and accurate.
2. The merchant made a false _________________ (accuse) against the young men.
3. The King's _________________ (recognise) of their talents led to a remarkable offer.
4. Each _________________ (deduce) was supported by clear physical evidence.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. observation; 2. accusation; 3. recognition; 4. deduction. A sample original sentence: 'The King's recognition of the young men's careful deduction impressed the entire court.'

items.source_context: Group enactment of 'Wisdom Paves the Way' with role assignment and oral delivery focus.
items.item_stem: Your group will perform Scene I of 'Wisdom Paves the Way' for the class. Before the performance, complete the following planning task in writing: (a) List the roles each group member will play. (b) Identify one line for each speaking character where sentence stress is especially important and explain why. (c) Name one stage direction from Scene I and describe how your group will carry it out physically.

expected_elements: Clear role list with every speaking character assigned to a group member.
Specific line identified per character with reasoned justification for stress choice.
Stage direction named and physical execution described concretely.
Writing demonstrates understanding of how vocal and physical choices serve the play's meaning.

items.source_lo: Student collaborates to stage a dramatic performance, applying vocal skills and production planning using the play as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Group enactment of 'Wisdom Paves the Way' with role assignment and oral delivery focus.
items.item_stem: Design a short production plan for staging 'Wisdom Paves the Way' in your school hall. Your plan should address: (a) how you would assign and prepare actors for Scene II (the court scene) with at least five named roles; (b) one set design decision that helps the audience understand the shift from the road to the royal court; (c) one sound or lighting choice for the moment when the King announces his verdict; and (d) how you would promote the performance to the school community. Present your plan as a short written document (approximately 150 words) using clear headings for each section.

expected_elements: Five or more named roles assigned with brief rationale for each casting choice.
Set design decision distinguishes road and court settings meaningfully.
Sound or lighting choice is linked specifically to the King's verdict moment.
Promotion idea is practical and suited to a school community context.
